name: Rental Turns
title: Rental Turn and Make-Ready Services | Genstone Construction
metaDescription: Rental turns and make-ready work between tenants: move-out documentation, standard turn scopes, upgrades at turnover and fast handoff back to leasing.
h1: Rental Turns and Make-Ready Between Tenants
lede: The days between one lease ending and the next one starting are the most expensive days a rental has: no rent coming in, utilities and taxes still due, and a property that cannot be shown until it is ready. Genstone Construction handles rental turns for owners, property managers and portfolio operators, from routine make-ready to heavier turns that fold in repairs and upgrades, with documentation that supports deposit decisions and capital planning.

sections.h2: Vacancy is the cost that matters most
sections.body:
On a stabilized rental, the turn is where operating performance is often decided. A house that sits empty while the owner chases a painter, waits for a flooring installer and argues with a cleaning crew about what was included can lose more rent than the turn itself costs. Multiply that across a portfolio and slow turns become one of the largest drags on returns.

A good turn process attacks vacancy from both ends. Before the resident leaves, it plans the work so crews and materials are ready on move-out day. After the resident leaves, it moves through inspection, scoping, approval, work and final cleaning without dead days between steps. And it delivers a home that leasing can photograph and show immediately, without a follow-up visit to fix what was missed.

That discipline is the same one we apply to renovation projects. Every turn has a defined scope, a designated field manager responsible for getting it done, and documentation of what was found and what was fixed. The difference is pace and volume. Turns are smaller, more frequent and more repetitive than renovations, so the process has to be lighter while staying consistent.

Genstone handles turns for individual landlords with a few homes as well as institutional owners with large single-family and small multifamily portfolios. Turn and make-ready work is also part of what Genstone Field Services provides, and depending on the scope and the client's setup, the two companies coordinate so routine make-ready and heavier construction work flow through one relationship.

Every turn starts with an accurate picture of the home's condition after the resident leaves. That inspection serves three purposes: it defines the turn scope, it supports decisions about the security deposit, and it adds to the property's long-term condition record.

The move-out inspection should be thorough and consistent. Our process covers each room systematically, including walls, ceilings, flooring, doors, windows, blinds, cabinets, countertops, fixtures, appliances, and heating and cooling equipment. It also covers the exterior, the yard, the garage and any outbuildings. Photos are taken from consistent positions and tied to specific findings.

Distinguishing normal wear from resident damage is one of the most important parts of the inspection, and one of the most frequently disputed. Faded paint, light scuffs, minor carpet wear in traffic paths and loosened hardware are typically normal wear. Holes in walls, burns, pet damage, broken fixtures, missing items and heavy soiling are typically damage. The documentation should make that distinction clear for each item, because the property manager will rely on it when accounting for the deposit.

Comparing the move-out condition to the move-in record is the most reliable way to support a damage claim. If your property manager has move-in photos and a condition report, we use them as the baseline. If not, the move-out documentation becomes the baseline for the next tenancy.

The inspection also looks beyond the resident's impact. It notes the age and condition of systems, flags items approaching replacement and identifies anything that should be addressed now rather than during the next tenancy.

Most turns follow a predictable pattern. Having a standard scope, adjusted for the specific home, saves time on every turn and keeps the quality consistent across the portfolio.

A typical make-ready scope covers:

- Paint: touch-up where walls are in good condition, full repaint of rooms with heavy wear or damage, using the portfolio's standard colors and sheens so touch-ups blend.
- Patching and drywall repair for holes, dents and anchor marks.
- Flooring: cleaning, repair of damaged sections, or replacement of worn carpet, ideally with durable hard surface flooring.
- Fixtures and hardware: repair or replacement of broken faucets, light fixtures, outlet covers, cabinet hardware, door handles and blinds.
- Appliances: cleaning, testing and repair or replacement of anything that fails.
- Life safety: testing and replacing smoke and carbon monoxide detectors as needed, checking GFCI outlets, and confirming handrails and locks are secure.
- Mechanical: replacing filters, checking heating and cooling operation, and flagging equipment that needs service.
- Rekeying or replacing locks.
- Pest treatment where needed.
- Exterior cleanup: landscaping, trash removal and a check of gutters, entry lighting and address numbers.
- A thorough final clean, including inside cabinets and appliances.

Debris and trash removal costs are included in the estimate. Items the resident left behind are documented before removal in case the property manager needs a record.

The standard scope is a starting point. Your field manager adjusts it for each home based on the move-out inspection and your instructions.

sections.h2: When a turn should become a renovation
sections.body:
A vacant home is the best time to do work that would be disruptive with a resident in place. The question at each turn is how much more to do beyond basic make-ready, and the answer depends on the home's condition, the rental market and your plans for the property.

Some items are clear candidates for the turn. Worn carpet should usually be replaced with durable hard surface flooring at turnover, not during a tenancy. Kitchen and bathroom updates, interior repainting in a new standard color, and replacing original fixtures and cabinets all fit naturally into a vacancy period. Items found during the move-out inspection that would likely fail during the next tenancy, such as a water heater near the end of its life or a deteriorating shower surround, are also worth addressing before a new resident moves in.

Sometimes the turn is an opportunity to reposition the home. If the rents for updated comparable homes nearby are meaningfully higher than what the property currently achieves, a targeted renovation at turnover may produce a return that a basic make-ready cannot. Our estimators can price an upgraded turn alongside the standard scope so you can compare the added cost against the expected rent increase and the added vacancy time.

The tradeoff is real: a bigger scope means more days without rent. For that reason, we recommend planning heavier turns in advance where possible, ideally once you know a resident is leaving, so materials can be ordered and crews scheduled before move-out. When a turn becomes a renovation, it receives a full scope document and estimate with a draw schedule, the same as any other Genstone project.

sections.h2: Planning before the resident moves out
sections.body:
The fastest turns begin before the keys come back. When the property manager knows a resident is leaving, a few steps can remove days from the vacancy period.

A pre-move-out walk, where the lease and local rules permit it, gives the field manager an early look at the condition of the home. It will not catch everything, because furniture and belongings hide damage, but it usually reveals whether the turn will be routine or heavy, whether flooring will need replacement, and whether any equipment is failing. That is enough to order long-lead materials and reserve crews.

Communication between the property manager and the turn team matters as much as the inspection. The field manager should know the move-out date, how access will be provided, any concerns the manager already has about the home, and the target date for the home to be ready for showings. The property manager should know the planned scope, any approvals needed, and the expected completion date.

Approvals are a common bottleneck. If the owner must approve every turn line by line, the turn waits on the owner's schedule. Many portfolio owners set an approval threshold or a pre-approved standard scope so routine turns proceed immediately and only exceptions require review. We work within whatever approval structure you use and make the exceptions easy to review with photos and clear line items.

If your homes are managed by Genstone Property Management, this coordination happens within the same company group, which removes a handoff between separate businesses. If you use another manager, we coordinate directly with their team.

For owners with more than a handful of homes, consistency is what makes turns efficient over time. When every home uses the same paint colors, flooring, fixtures, hardware and appliances, turns get faster because crews know what to expect, materials can be stocked in advance, and repairs blend with existing finishes instead of creating a patchwork.

If you have a written rent-ready standard, we turn every home to it. If you do not, the turn process is a good place to start building one. Each turn becomes an opportunity to replace nonstandard items with standard ones, and over several turnover cycles the portfolio converges on a consistent specification.

Consistency also applies to how turns are documented. Move-out inspections, photos, scopes, costs and completion records should be organized the same way for every home. That makes it possible to compare turn costs across homes and markets, identify homes that consistently cost more to turn, and see patterns, such as particular floor types or fixtures that fail repeatedly, that point to better specifications.

Over time, turn records become one of the most useful data sources an owner has. They show which homes are aging well, which need capital investment, and which residents and property types tend to produce heavier turns. Combined with renovation records, they give asset managers a clear picture of each home's condition history.

Genstone's field managers apply the same quality checks to turns as to renovations, and finished work is reviewed against your standard before the home is released to leasing.

Each turn has a designated field manager who oversees the work from move-out inspection to final clean and serves as the point of contact for you and your property manager. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed and insured local contractors from a national network of thousands, so turns in different markets follow the same process and standard.

You receive the move-out documentation, the turn scope and estimate, progress updates and completion photos without needing to visit the home. Where a turn requires permits, such as electrical, plumbing or mechanical replacements, our team coordinates them. Contractor insurance and licensing are verified, and lien waivers are collected on larger scopes.

No upfront payment is required. Work is billed against completed scope, and final billing follows completion and your approval. Completed work carries a one-year workmanship warranty. Damage caused by residents and normal wear and tear are not covered, which is why durable materials and consistent standards matter so much on rentals.

Turns are part of a broader ownership cycle, and the Genstone Companies cover much of it. Genstone Field Services provides turn and make-ready services, property inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance. Genstone Property Management handles marketing, leasing, resident screening, rent collection and maintenance coordination. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans and lines of credit for portfolio growth, and Genstone Insurance provides rental and multi-property coverage. Each can be used independently.

To set up turn service for one home or an entire portfolio, call (312) 429-2637.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a turn and a renovation?
faqs.a: A turn is the work needed to make a home ready for the next resident: cleaning, paint, repairs, fixture replacement, life-safety checks and similar items. A renovation goes further, such as updating a kitchen, replacing flooring throughout or replacing major systems. Many turns include some renovation work, because a vacant home is the best time for it. Heavier turns receive a full scope, estimate and draw schedule like any other Genstone project.

faqs.q: Can your move-out documentation support security deposit deductions?
faqs.a: Our move-out inspections document the condition of each room with consistent photos and separate normal wear from resident damage item by item. That record gives your property manager clear support for deposit accounting. The comparison is strongest when there is a move-in condition report and photos to compare against. Deposit decisions themselves are made by the owner or property manager under the lease and applicable rules.

faqs.q: How do you keep turns from taking too long?
faqs.a: By planning before move-out where possible, using a standard scope so crews and materials are ready, working within approval thresholds so routine items proceed without waiting, and keeping one field manager accountable for moving the turn from inspection to final clean without dead days. Heavier turns that include upgrades are scoped in advance so long-lead materials are ordered before the home is vacant.

faqs.q: Should I replace carpet at every turn?
faqs.a: Not necessarily at every turn, but when carpet is worn, stained or damaged, replacing it with durable hard surface flooring at turnover usually makes sense for a rental. Waterproof plank or tile holds up better, cleans more easily and often needs only spot repair at later turns. We price the options during the move-out inspection so you can decide based on condition and your rent-ready standard.

faqs.q: Do you handle turns for small multifamily buildings?
faqs.a: Yes. We turn individual units in duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes as well as single-family homes. In occupied buildings, turn work is scheduled with the other residents in mind, especially when it involves noise, shared areas or shutdowns of shared systems. The move-out inspection also notes building-wide items visible from the unit, such as roof leaks or plumbing issues affecting neighboring units.

faqs.q: Does Genstone Field Services also do turns?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services offers turn and make-ready services along with property preservation, inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance. Depending on the scope and how your portfolio is set up, routine make-ready and heavier construction work can be coordinated between Genstone Field Services and Genstone Construction so you have one relationship covering both, without managing separate vendors for each type of turn.

faqs.q: Is turn work covered by a warranty?
faqs.a: Completed work carries Genstone's one-year workmanship warranty. Damage caused by residents and normal wear and tear are not covered, so a fixture broken by the next resident would not fall under the warranty, while a repair that fails because of how it was installed would. That distinction is one reason we recommend durable materials and consistent standards across rental homes.
